newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon chambers of commerce challenge Hariri.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon chambers of commerce challenge Hariri.

text.p: Lebanon's chambers of commerce called on Wednesday for a showdown with Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri over government decisions to restrict imports which they see as a threat to the country's liberal economic system.

Representatives of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry said they regretted the decisions to raise car import duties and ban some food imports and said they would not tolerate any attempt to alter Lebanon's liberal economic system.

They said in a statement that last week's decisions to raise duty on luxury cars to 200 percent and ban import of foods already grown in Lebanon could have negative implications for the economy and expressed regret that they had not been consulted.

"The chambers of commerce are anxious to maintain the essence of the liberal economic system adopted by Lebanon until today and will not tolerate any attempt to touch the essential foundations of this system," the statement said.

They were the second business group this week to challenge the decisions, which are designed to reduce Lebanon's massive trade deficit and stimulate agriculture but have been denounced as the start of a trend away from economic liberalism.

The Lebanese Business Managers Grouping representing 300 businessmen across the country on Monday called the decisions improvised, ill-considered and hasty and demanded that the government maintain economic liberalism.
Going a step further, the chambers of commerce demanded a meeting with Hariri "to explain the damage incurred on the economy and on the social situation by the implementation of the decisions".

They said they would ask Hariri to set up a national economic council from the public and private sector to propose the general direction of the economy, draft policies and co-ordinate their implementation.
The statement said they also called for a clear agricultural policy with specific targets and time frames.

The government's decision to restrict food imports from October has been criticised as more likely to encourage smuggling, inflation and a decline in the quality of Lebanese agricultural products than to stimulate agriculture unless it is accompanied by new investment and development policies.
